title: Wolff rearrangement (Arndt–Eistert)
subtitle: A diazoketone loses N₂ to a ketene, which water turns into phenylacetic acid

reactants.caption: a diazoketone, PhCOCHN₂ (drawn as C⁻–N⁺≡N), in aqueous dioxane
reactants.learnerPrompt: Heat: N₂ leaves and a group moves.
hintTiers: N₂ is an excellent leaving group. When it leaves, the carbon is short of electrons. Which group on the carbonyl carbon next door can move across?
Three arrows: the C–N bond breaks onto nitrogen, the phenyl moves from the carbonyl carbon to the carbon that lost N₂, and that carbon's lone pair makes a C=C bond to the carbonyl carbon.
C–N bond → a lone pair on nitrogen (N₂ leaves); bond from the carbonyl carbon to the ring → new bond from the ring carbon to the CHN₂ carbon; lone pair on that carbon → C=C π bond.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Water adding to the ketone only gives a hydrate, which reverts. On heating the diazoketone first loses N₂.
N₂ leaves as a neutral molecule, taking the C–N bonding pair with it.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: N₂ leaves and phenyl moves. The carbonyl carbon is now short of electrons: use the lone pair on the other carbon to make a C=C bond.

acylcarbene.caption: an acylcarbene + N₂
hintTiers: The carbene carbon has an empty p orbital. A group on the next carbon can move into it.
Two arrows: the phenyl moves to the carbene carbon, and the carbene lone pair makes a C=C bond to the carbonyl carbon.
Bond from the carbonyl carbon to the ring → new bond from the ring carbon to the carbene carbon; carbene lone pair → C=C π bond.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Carbenes can insert into O–H bonds, but here the 1,2-shift is faster. Move the phenyl group.

ketene.caption: phenylketene, PhCH=C=O + N₂
hintTiers: The central carbon of C=C=O is very electrophilic, like the carbon of an isocyanate. Water is the nucleophile.
The water oxygen bonds to the central carbon, and the C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. Two arrows.
Water lone pair → new bond to the central ketene carbon; C=O π bond → a lone pair on oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The CH end of the ketene is electron-rich. Water bonds to the central carbon, between the C=C and the C=O.
N₂ is unreactive and bubbles away. Water adds to the ketene.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: water bonds to the central carbon. That carbon now has five bonds: move the C=O π pair onto oxygen.

zwitterion.caption: the water adduct: an enolate with a positive oxygen
zwitterion.learnerPrompt: A second water removes a proton.
hintTiers: The added oxygen carries two hydrogens and a positive charge. Which base is present?
The second water takes a drawn proton from the positive oxygen; the O–H pair stays on that oxygen. Two arrows.
Second water lone pair → new bond to a drawn H on the positive oxygen; that O–H bond → a lone pair on oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Losing water just returns the ketene. Remove a proton instead.

enolate.caption: the enolate of phenylacetic acid + H₃O⁺
hintTiers: An enolate can be protonated on oxygen or on carbon. Protonation on carbon gives the carboxylic acid directly.
Three arrows: the C=C π pair takes a proton from H₃O⁺, the O–H pair stays on the water oxygen, and the O⁻ lone pair re-forms C=O.
C=C π bond → new bond from the CH carbon to an H of H₃O⁺; that O–H bond → a lone pair on the water oxygen; O⁻ lone pair → C=O π bond.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Protonating oxygen gives the enediol, which tautomerises to the same acid, but that is a longer way round. Protonate the carbon.
Push the C=C π pair to a proton, not onto a carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: carbon takes the proton. The central carbon would be left with a positive charge: the O⁻ lone pair re-forms C=O.

steps.explanationAfterStep: N₂ leaves as the phenyl group moves to the electron-poor carbon next door, giving a ketene: the Wolff rearrangement. A diazoketone that can adopt the s-cis conformation is thought to lose N₂ and rearrange in one step.
Also accepted: N₂ leaves first, giving a free acylcarbene. Carbenes from diazoketones (made with heat, light or a silver catalyst) can rearrange this way, and some are trapped by other reagents.
The phenyl group moves into the empty orbital of the carbene, with its bonding pair: a 1,2-shift that gives the ketene.
Water adds to the central carbon of the ketene, giving an enolate.
A second water molecule takes a proton from the positive oxygen.
Protonation on carbon gives phenylacetic acid: benzoic acid has been homologated to the next acid in the series.

mechanismSummary: The diazoketone (made from benzoyl chloride and diazomethane) loses N₂ on heating, and the phenyl group moves to the carbon that lost it: the Wolff rearrangement gives phenylketene. Water adds to the ketene, and proton transfers give phenylacetic acid, one CH₂ longer than benzoic acid: the Arndt–Eistert homologation. In practice the rearrangement is usually catalysed by silver(I) (Ag₂O or silver benzoate) or driven by light; silver is not drawn here, as the app has no transition-metal steps. With an alcohol instead of water, the product is the ester.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 38
